paras.sec_title: Introduction
paras.text: The undergraduate stage represents a critical window of vulnerability for the onset and escalation of mental health disorders (Zhang et al., 2025a). Epidemiological evidence indicates that the global pooled prevalence rates of depressive and anxiety symptoms among college students are as high as 33.6% and 39.0%, respectively—levels that are significantly elevated compared to their non-student peers (Li et al., 2022). Negative emotional symptoms, including depression, anxiety, and stress, not only severely impair academic performance, social adaptation, and overall quality of life among undergraduate students, but also precipitate long-term psychosomatic health risks (Zada et al., 2021; Kusumaningsih, 2016; McCloughen et al., 2012), imposing a profound clinical and economic burden on global public health systems (Collaborators, 2022). Consequently, identifying modifiable, actionable factors to facilitate early prevention of psychological distress has emerged as a paramount objective for health promotion initiatives within higher education worldwide.

paras.sec_title: Introduction
paras.text: Among a myriad of non-pharmacological interventions, physical activity and physical fitness have garnered substantial academic attention due to their multi-systemic health benefits (Elbe et al., 2019). Cumulative evidence suggests that habitual physical activity is inversely associated with the risk of depressive, anxious, and stress symptoms, and structured exercise interventions have been empirically validated as effective modalities for mitigating mental health problems in college populations (Singh et al., 2023). Recently, a paradigm shift has occurred in the literature; research focus is progressively transitioning from subjective, self-reported metrics—such as exercise frequency and duration—toward the objective and granular evaluation of multidimensional physical fitness components, including cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength, speed, endurance, and flexibility (Banyard et al., 2025). Rather than serving as mere markers of physical capacity, these objective fitness indices play a pivotal role in constructing a physiological buffer against psychological stressors. This protective mechanism is hypothesized to operate by reshaping the neuroendocrine microenvironment, optimizing sleep architecture, and enhancing physical self-efficacy (Lubans et al., 2016).

paras.sec_title: Physical fitness assessment
paras.text: Objective physical fitness data were obtained through supervised, on-site field testing (Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China, 2014), strictly adhering to the protocols and operational guidelines outlined in the National Student Physical Health Standard (2014 Revision) (hereafter referred to as the Standard). The assessment battery covered three domains—physiological function, physical capacity, and somatic morphology—whereas the analytic PFI used in the present study was restricted to indicators of physiological function and physical capacity. Somatic morphology was assessed separately using BMI.

paras.sec_title: Physical fitness assessment
paras.text: Subsequently, the individual Z-scores were aggregated to composite the global Physical Fitness Index (PFI) (Li et al., 2020). Given that the 50-meter sprint and the 1,000-meter/800-meter endurance runs are time-dependent metrics (where higher values denote lower physical performance), their standardized scores were reverse-scored (multiplied by−1) prior to composite calculation. paras.sec_title: Physical fitness assessment
paras.text: A higher PFI score represents better comprehensive physical fitness. To account for sex-specific performance distributions, PFI categories were defined separately within female and male students using the sex-specific sample percentiles (Yang and Ma, 2024). Low PFI was <P25, moderate PFI was P25–P75 (inclusive), and high PFI was >P75.

paras.sec_title: Assessment of depression, anxiety, and stress
paras.text: Negative emotional symptoms among college students were evaluated using the 21-item Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS-21), originally developed by Lovibond and Lovibond (1995) and psychometrically validated for Chinese populations by Gong et al. (2010). This instrument has demonstrated robust reliability and validity across diverse demographic cohorts.

paras.sec_title: Assessment of depression, anxiety, and stress
paras.text: In the present dataset, Cronbach's α was 0.931 for the total DASS-21 and 0.853, 0.810, and 0.844 for the stress, anxiety, and depression subscales, respectively. For prevalence and regression analyses, each subscale was dichotomized as 0 = normal and 1 = mild-or-higher symptoms, using thresholds of ≥15 for stress, ≥8 for anxiety, and ≥10 for depression (Zhang et al., 2025b).

The raw scores from weekdays and weekends were aggregated to yield a cumulative weekly MVPA score ranging from 0 to 7 days. This psychometric assessment protocol has demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability (Intraclass Correlation Coefficient, ICC = 0.82 (Liu et al., 2010) and desirable criterion validity against accelerometer-measured metrics (r = 0.40) (Prochaska et al., 2001) within Chinese youth populations.

paras.sec_title: Statistical analysis
paras.text: All overall models adjusted for sex, BMI category, weekly MVPA days (Larouche et al., 2014), weekly MSE days (Guo and Rao, 2021), autonomous exercise frequency, organized sports participation, daily screen-time category, and daily sedentary-time category. Sex-stratified models omitted sex. MVPA and MSE were modeled linearly per additional day/week; the remaining behavioral variables and BMI were categorical. Reference levels were female sex, normal BMI, 0 autonomous exercise sessions/week, 0 organized sports sessions/week, no screen time, and no sedentary time. All tests were two-sided, with P < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

paras.sec_title: Prevalence of negative emotional symptoms and the protective role of physical fitness metrics
paras.text: These symptom-detection rates require comparison with external evidence. The anxiety detection rate in this sample (67.67%) was substantially higher than the global pooled estimate of 39.0% (95% CI 34.6%−43.4%) reported for college students, whereas the depression rate (12.37%) was lower than the corresponding pooled estimate of 33.6% (95% CI 29.3%−37.8%) (Li et al., 2022). That meta-analysis did not provide a directly comparable pooled stress estimate. Accordingly, the present stress and anxiety figures should not be generalized as clinical prevalence without considering instrument, threshold, sampling, and timing differences. This observation implies that the psychological distress burden among contemporary undergraduate populations remains profoundly elevated, a finding that is highly congruent with the global reports by Wang X et al., who documented that over 70% of surveyed international college students experienced marked escalations in anxiety and stress driven by academic pressures and environmental uncertainties (Gao et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).

paras.sec_title: Prevalence of negative emotional symptoms and the protective role of physical fitness metrics
paras.text: Data were collected between December 2025 and January 2026, overlapping with end-of-term academic and physical-fitness assessments. This context may have contributed to short-term stress and anxiety, but the present cross-sectional data cannot quantify that contribution. The clustered sample of second-year students from Chongqing may also differ from samples included in international meta-analyses (Wang et al., 2016).

paras.sec_title: Prevalence of negative emotional symptoms and the protective role of physical fitness metrics
paras.text: Academic competition, employment concerns, digital lifestyles, and social adaptation are plausible contextual stressors (Zhang et al., 2025c; Elhai et al., 2017), but they were not all measured in this study. They should therefore be treated as possible explanations rather than demonstrated causes of the high stress and anxiety detection rates.

paras.sec_title: Prevalence of negative emotional symptoms and the protective role of physical fitness metrics
paras.text: The cornerstone innovation of the present study lies in the revelation that the robust, independent inverse associations between the global PFI and the risks of manifesting three distinct negative emotional symptoms persisted, even after a comprehensive suite of behavioral exercise variables (MVPA, MSE, autonomous exercise, and organized sports participation) and critical lifestyle confounders (screen time, sedentary duration, and BMI classifications) were systematically adjusted for. Compared with the low PFI tier, individuals in the moderate and high PFI groups exhibited pronounced reductions in psychological distress risks. This crucial empirical insight strongly corroborates the ongoing paradigm shift currently advocated within the international scientific community—namely, the conceptual transition from behavioral engagement to physiological function in mental health epidemiology (Dishman et al., 2015; Kandola et al., 2019; Schuch et al., 2018). However, this study several categorical ORs for the high-PFI group were extremely small, positive outcome cells were sparse, and some Hosmer–Lemeshow tests indicated possible calibration limitations. Although the conventional, Firth-penalized, and continuous-PFI analyses were directionally consistent, the exact magnitudes of the extreme categorical ORs should be interpreted cautiously and should not be regarded as precise causal effect estimates. In addition, because Tables 1, 2 represent separate association models rather than formal comparisons of predictive performance, the results do not establish that PFI predicts mental health outcomes better than its individual components or exercise behavior. PFI should therefore be viewed as a complementary composite indicator whose predictive and clinical utility requires prospective external validation.

paras.sec_title: Prevalence of negative emotional symptoms and the protective role of physical fitness metrics
paras.text: PFI provides a complementary composite representation of cardiorespiratory, neuromuscular, and flexibility domains. Prospective validation and direct model-comparison studies would be needed to establish incremental predictive value. While a vast body of historical literature has remained predominantly anchored in subjective, self-reported behavioral indices (i.e., mapping “how long or how frequently” an individual exercises), our findings provide compelling evidence that an individual's objectively verified, accrued PFI possesses significantly superior predictive and protective power for mental health than mere exercise frequency or behavioral participation alone (Kandola et al., 2020). This disparity can be elucidated by the fact that the comprehensive Physical Fitness Index integrates multi-systemic physiological capacities, including cardiorespiratory efficacy and neuromuscular adaptation. Consequently, rather than being a mere reflection of acute lifestyle habits, the PFI represents the ultimate phenotypic physiological manifestation of a complex, long-term interaction among an individual's genetic endowment, habitual physical behaviors, and environmental exposures. It essentially serves as a robust, resilient somatic buffer that shields the central nervous system against external psychological stressors.

paras.sec_title: Mechanistic insights: biological, behavioral, and psychosocial pathways
paras.text: The Biological Dimension (Neuroendocrine Remodeling): Sustained optimal physical fitness induces a profound remodeling of the central nervous and endocrine microenvironments. Physically fit individuals exhibit enhanced neurotrophic support within the central nervous system, characterized by the upregulated synthesis and release of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), alongside optimized neurochemical pathways for dopamine and serotonin (5−HT) (Cotman et al., 2007). Concurrently, the CSA hypothesis posits that high-PFI individuals possess a more resilient and tightly regulated hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. When exposed to psychological stressors, these individuals exhibit a blunted, adaptive cortisol response and a downstream down regulation of systemic pro-inflammatory cytokines—such as interleukin-6 (IF−6) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF−∝)—thereby biophysically obstructing the pathophysiological cascade of anxiety and depression (Schuch et al., 2019).

paras.sec_title: Mechanistic insights: biological, behavioral, and psychosocial pathways
paras.text: The Behavioral and Psychological Dimension (Sleep Architecture and Recovery): High cardiorespiratory and muscular fitness are naturally coupled with optimized sleep architecture, characterized by higher sleep efficiency and a greater proportion of slow-wave (deep) sleep. This superior sleep quality serves as a direct homeostatic mechanism that repairs accumulated daytime neural fatigue and mitigates emotional depletion (Kredlow et al., 2015).

paras.sec_title: Mechanistic insights: biological, behavioral, and psychosocial pathways
paras.text: The Social Dimension (Identity Reconstruction and Social Capital): Objective physical competencies directly enhance individual “body image,” which in turn boosts physical self-efficacy and core self-esteem. Furthermore, higher-fitness individuals naturally garner greater opportunities for prosocial interaction and peer support, constructing a rich reservoir of psychosocial resources that effectively buffers academic and adaptive stressors (Fox, 2003). It should be pointed out that although this study provides theoretical explanations for these mechanisms, it does not directly test the statistical mediation effect. In this regard, the results of this study are consistent with recent evidence formally testing such mediation paths: Zhao et al. (2025) confirmed in a sample of China college students that self-esteem significantly mediates the relationship between physical activity and depression and anxiety symptoms, providing direct empirical support for the “identity reconstruction” hypothesis proposed in this paper.

paras.sec_title: The dominance of cardiorespiratory fitness and the novel contribution of somatic flexibility
paras.text: When dissecting individual components via multivariable Logistic regression, speed (50-meter sprint) and cardiorespiratory endurance (800/1,000-meter runs) emerged as the most prominent predictors of negative emotional symptoms. Within sports sciences, these two performance metrics serve as core field-based proxies for cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF). Our study demonstrated that, irrespective of gender, prolonged completion times in these running events (indicative of depleted CRF) significantly elevated the risks of stress and anxiety detection. This empirical pattern highlights CRF as a highly sensitive fitness domain within the brain's central emotion-regulation networks. Suboptimal CRF not only signifies compromised aerobic oxidative capacity and restricted fatigue reserves, but also triggers a cascade of diminished exercise self-confidence and the chronic somatic accumulation of daytime fatigue, ultimately rendering the individual's psychological defense mechanisms vulnerable to collapse under chronic academic strain (Kandola et al., 2019; Dishman et al., 2015).

paras.sec_title: The dominance of cardiorespiratory fitness and the novel contribution of somatic flexibility
paras.text: Concurrently, vital capacity, muscular strength (pull-ups/sit-ups), and flexibility (sit-and-reach) displayed consistent protective associations. While vital capacity reflects respiratory system reserve and oxygen kinetics, muscular strength indicates the functional capacity of the neuromuscular system—a finding that strongly supports the burgeoning global clinical paradigm favoring resistance training as a primary non-pharmacological intervention for psychiatric disorders (Gordon et al., 2018).

paras.sec_title: The dominance of cardiorespiratory fitness and the novel contribution of somatic flexibility
paras.text: Notably, the significant association observed between flexibility (the sit-and-reach test)—traditionally regarded as a rudimentary baseline component—and the mitigation of stress and anxiety offers profound academic insights. This phenomenon can be elegantly elucidated by the somatization activation theory. Chronic psychological distress and anxiety frequently manifest physically as persistent, generalized neuromuscular tension (somatization symptoms). Individuals possessing superior musculoskeletal flexibility inherently exhibit lower resting muscle tension. This structural laxity is hypothesized to downregulate central anxiety alarms via the counter-activation of the parasympathetic nervous system, thereby enhancing subjective somatic comfort and restoring emotional homeostasis (Behm et al., 2026).

paras.sec_title: Gender-specific divergence in the fitness-mental health nexus
paras.text: In male students, depressive symptoms exhibited a highly localized sensitivity to performance-based, explosive physical metrics, specifically the 50-meter sprint and the 1,000-meter run, where sub-optimal performance significantly exacerbated the risk of depression. This empirical phenomenon is deeply anchored in traditional gender role expectations and competitive achievement motivation. Within contemporary campus subcultures, speed and cardiorespiratory endurance are rarely interpreted as mere physiological indicators; rather, they are heavily heavily operationalized as socially constructed markers of “athletic prowess,” “dominance,” and “masculine competence” (Sharp et al., 2024). Consequently, a deficit in these high-visibility, performance-driven fitness categories can easily induce a state of chronic exercise-related inferiority, body dissatisfaction, and perceived physical incompetence among male undergraduates, ultimately precipitating the clinical cascade into anhedonia and depressive manifestations.

paras.sec_title: Gender-specific divergence in the fitness-mental health nexus
paras.text: Conversely, female students manifested a distinct, multi-dimensional holistic protective pattern. Although no single, isolated physical fitness metric reached statistical significance in predicting depressive symptoms among females, their global aggregated PFI demonstrated an exceptionally robust, protective threshold against all three negative emotional domains. This striking contrast implies that the psychological resilience of female college students does not depend on singular, high-performance athletic indices, but is rather sustained by a synergistic, multi-systemic baseline health matrix that encapsulates cardiorespiratory reserve, muscular capacity, and somatic flexibility in unison (Xu et al., 2026). For the female cohort, psychological wellbeing appears to be anchored in the overall harmony of the somatic profile rather than isolated competitive excellence, a finding that underscores the necessity of adopting a holistic health-quality paradigm—rather than a performance-centric sports model—when developing targeted mental health interventions for female college students. Similarly, Levante et al. (2024) reported in a sample of female college students that the protective effect of physical exercise habits on psychological distress is mediated by multiple physiological and psychosocial factors, a finding that is highly consistent with the “holistic” female pattern observed in this study and suggests that future research should explicitly test multiple mediation models rather than just relying on direct associations.

paras.sec_title: Behavioral nuances of digital lifestyles and targeted practical implications
paras.text: Within the domain of digital lifestyle indicators, the intriguing juxtaposition wherein “screen time exhibited no statistical correlation, while sedentary duration was significantly tied to anxiety and depression” aligns seamlessly with cutting-edge behavioral epidemiology. Non-academic screen engagement operates as a double-edged sword (Choukas-Bradley et al., 2023; Van de Casteele et al., 2026). While screen use inevitably triggers a “displacement effect” that reduces physical activity time, the intrinsic nature of the content—ranging from immersive social networking and hyper-interactive gaming to short-form entertainment—frequently offers a mechanism for hedonic escape or psychological compensation. This digital coping strategy may dilute or neutralize its potential psychopathological side effects (Choukas-Bradley et al., 2023; Van de Casteele et al., 2026). Conversely, prolonged sedentary behavior constitutes an independent risk factor distinct from physical inactivity. An absolute, prolonged state of low energy expenditure severely suppresses baseline metabolic kinetics, dampens central nervous system arousal, and accelerates the somatic accumulation of fatigue, thereby directly biophysically catalyzing the onset of anxious and depressive symptoms (Subiron-Valera et al., 2023).
